scenarios.scenario: Engineers kick off long agent runs and switch to other windows. They want an OS desktop alert the moment the run is blocked waiting for an approval or for input, without anyone watching the terminal.

key.primary: Notification hook, with matchers for notification types such as permission_prompt and idle_prompt, whose command fires the OS notifier
key.rejected_alternative: A Stop hook that sends the alert when Claude finishes responding
key.rejection_reason: Stop fires only when Claude ends its turn. A session blocked mid-turn on a permission prompt has not stopped, so a Stop-based alert never fires at the moment attention is actually needed. Notification is the documented event for permission prompts and idle waiting, and the hooks guide's first walkthrough is exactly this desktop-alert use case.
key.context_boundary: no context window (the notifier is a pure side-effect command fired on the Notification event); nothing crosses back into the conversation: the event supports no decision control, and even blocking stderr is shown to the user only, never to Claude
key.lifecycle: Notification event fires whenever Claude Code sends a notification; the matcher selects types like permission_prompt or idle_prompt
key.failure_mode: Notification hook output and exit code are ignored by design, so a broken notifier command fails completely silently: no alert and no surfaced error.

sheets.primary: A Notification hook with matcher permission_prompt, plus idle_prompt and agent_needs_input for background runs, whose command handler returns terminalSequence carrying an OSC 9, 99 or 777 desktop notification escape (or shells out to the platform notifier).
sheets.rejected_alternative: A Stop hook. It fires when Claude finishes responding, not when the run is parked waiting for an approval mid turn, so it would alert at the wrong moment and miss the blocked state entirely.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code raises the notification event and runs the handler, so the alert does not depend on the model noticing or announcing that it is blocked.
sheets.context_boundary: The handler runs in a separate process with the notification JSON (message, title, notification_type) on stdin. Nothing needs to reach the model; terminalSequence is emitted through Claude Code's own terminal write path rather than by the handler.
sheets.lifecycle: Fires each time Claude Code emits a notification of the matched type, for the life of the session, and stops when the hook entry is removed or hooks are disabled.
sheets.failure_mode: Advisory by construction: Notification hooks cannot block or modify anything, so a broken handler simply means the engineer never hears the ping, and it fails open. An escape sequence outside the allowlist is silently ignored, and hooks have no controlling terminal, so writing to /dev/tty instead of terminalSequence fails.
sheets.version_caveat: terminalSequence requires Claude Code v2.1.141 or later. The agent_needs_input and agent_completed matchers require v2.1.198 and only fire while agent view is open in a terminal, so background runs need that window open.

sheets.primary: A Notification hook in user settings with two matchers, permission_prompt and idle_prompt, each running an OS notifier; or, to avoid a platform-specific notifier binary, a hook that returns a terminalSequence containing an OSC 9 or OSC 777 notification escape that Claude Code emits through its own terminal write path.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A Stop hook. It fires when the main agent has finished responding, which is the end of a turn, not the moment mid-run when the agent is parked on an approval dialog, so it would miss precisely the event the engineers want to be paged about.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. Claude Code raises the notification event itself and runs the registered handler; the model is not consulted and cannot suppress or forget the alert.
sheets.context_boundary: A separate process outside the conversation. The event JSON carrying message, title, notification_type, session_id, and transcript_path crosses in on stdin; nothing crosses into the model's context, and the hook's stderr is shown to the user only.
sheets.lifecycle: Fires every time Claude Code raises a notification whose type matches, for the life of the session: permission_prompt when Claude needs a tool approved, idle_prompt when Claude is done and waiting for the next prompt. It stops when the hook is removed from settings.
sheets.failure_mode: Purely advisory and fails open. Notification hooks cannot block or modify anything, so a notifier that is absent, unauthorized by the OS, or erroring simply drops the alert with no signal in the conversation. Hooks also run with no controlling terminal, so a handler that writes escape sequences straight to /dev/tty silently fails.
sheets.version_caveat: The terminalSequence field requires Claude Code v2.1.141 or later, and only OSC 0/1/2/9/99/777 and BEL are allowed through. The agent_needs_input and agent_completed matchers require v2.1.198 or later and fire only while agent view is open in a terminal, so do not rely on them for the ordinary terminal case.

sheets.primary: A Notification hook in settings.json that shells out to the platform's desktop notifier (osascript / notify-send / a Windows toast helper) using the message text supplied on the hook's stdin.
sheets.rejected_alternative: The built-in terminal bell / notification-channel setting, which is fine as a fallback but cannot be routed to a real OS toast or to a phone, and is easy to miss in a backgrounded terminal.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness fires the event; delivery beyond that is owned by the OS notification daemon, so the guarantee is only as good as the notifier.
sheets.context_boundary: The notifier runs outside the model context entirely and consumes only the event payload (message, session id, cwd). Nothing crosses back in; the hook should exit zero silently so the waiting turn is not disturbed.
sheets.lifecycle: Runs when Claude Code raises a notification event, which is the idle-waiting and permission-prompt case, and stops when the session ends or the user answers the prompt.
sheets.failure_mode: Advisory and fails open: if the notifier is not installed, the user's Do Not Disturb is on, or the event is not raised for the particular blocking state, the run simply sits there and no one is told. It can also be noisy, and a hook that blocks or takes seconds to return will visibly stall the prompt.
sheets.version_caveat: Which situations raise the Notification event (permission requests only, versus also long-idle input waits) has varied between releases, and I cannot confirm the current event coverage or its exact payload field names without the documentation; verify against the installed version rather than assuming both cases fire.

sheets.primary: A Notification hook in each engineer's ~/.claude/settings.json with matcher "permission_prompt" (add a second group with "idle_prompt" to also catch the waiting-for-your-next-prompt case), running the platform's native notifier: osascript on macOS, notify-send on Linux, or a PowerShell toast or MessageBox on Windows.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A PermissionRequest hook. It fires at the right moment but its job is to answer the permission decision, and wiring notification logic into it risks a hook that accidentally allows or defers prompts instead of merely announcing them.
sheets.enforcement_owner: Shared: the harness deterministically fires the Notification event and spawns the command, but the OS notification daemon owns actual delivery, so a fired hook is not a guaranteed alert.
sheets.context_boundary: The hook command runs in a separate process with the notification payload on stdin; nothing enters or leaves the model's context window. The run stays blocked in the CLI waiting for the human either way.
sheets.lifecycle: Fires each time Claude Code emits a notification of the matched type, for the life of every session on that machine, and stops at session end. The agent_needs_input and agent_completed matchers additionally only fire while agent view is open, so they are not a substitute for permission_prompt.
sheets.failure_mode: Purely advisory and fails open: a missed alert never blocks or delays the run, it just leaves the session stalled longer. osascript fails silently unless Script Editor has been granted notification permission, notify-send needs a running notification daemon, and a session over SSH, in a container, or headless with -p has no desktop to notify at all.
sheets.version_caveat: No version gate for the Notification event or the permission_prompt and idle_prompt matchers; agent_needs_input and agent_completed require Claude Code v2.1.198 or later. Because the notify command is platform-specific, this belongs in user settings rather than a shared repository settings file, or it will be a broken command on half the fleet.

scenarios.scenario: We run the agent in a fully auto-approved configuration for speed, but any git push must still halt and wait for a human to explicitly confirm, every single time, no matter what approval configuration the session is running under.

key.primary: A permissions ask rule such as Bash(git push *), which forces a confirmation prompt on every matching call
key.rejected_alternative: A PreToolUse hook returning permissionDecision "ask" for git push commands
key.rejection_reason: bypassPermissions mode skips prompts except a documented exception list: explicit ask rules, connector tools an organization set to ask, and MCP tools marked requiresUserInteraction. Hook ask decisions are not on that list, so they carry no documented guarantee of surviving prompt-skipping modes, whereas content-scoped ask rules are additionally documented to force a prompt even for sandboxed commands in auto-allow mode.
key.context_boundary: no context window (the rule is evaluated by the harness before the matching Bash call and pauses it on a terminal prompt); what crosses the boundary is the human's confirmation or refusal rather than model output, and the tool call proceeds only after that approval
key.lifecycle: evaluated before every matching Bash call in the fixed deny, then ask, then allow order; the prompt fires even in bypassPermissions and sandbox auto-allow
key.failure_mode: The gate requires a human present: in headless -p runs nobody can answer the prompt, and in dontAsk mode the call is denied outright instead of prompted, so unattended pipelines stall or fail at the gate.

sheets.primary: An explicit permissions.ask rule, Bash(git push *), placed in managed settings so no developer can drop it. Ask rules are evaluated ahead of allow rules and are one of the few things that still forces a prompt in bypassPermissions and auto mode, which is exactly the "no matter what approval configuration" requirement.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A PreToolUse hook on Bash returning permissionDecision "ask". It works, but it adds a script that can crash or be removed, and hook decisions never override the rule layer anyway, so the declarative ask rule is the mechanism the permission evaluator honours by construction.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness forces the prompt; the human owns the decision. The model has no way to skip it, and neither does the session's permission mode.
sheets.context_boundary: Entirely inside the harness's permission evaluation, before the Bash tool call is dispatched. The command string is rendered to the human in the prompt, and only the approve or deny outcome crosses back to the model as a tool result.
sheets.lifecycle: Evaluated on every Bash tool call for the whole session, in deny then ask then allow order, before any auto-approval path. It stops applying only if the rule is removed or if the command text does not match the pattern.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed for anything that matches, but the string match is the weak point and everything around it fails open: a push reached through an environment runner such as devbox run git push, a git alias, or a shell script the agent invokes never matches Bash(git push *). In dontAsk mode a call that would prompt is denied instead of prompted, which is safe but is not the requested "halt and wait for a human".
sheets.version_caveat: No version gate, plan restriction, or enabling flag applies to a content-scoped ask rule; it survives bypassPermissions, auto mode, and sandboxing with autoAllowBashIfSandboxed on. If you implement the same intent as a PreToolUse hook instead, v2.1.211 is the floor at which a hook's "ask" reliably forces the prompt in auto mode.

sheets.primary: An explicit ask rule in settings, permissions.ask containing Bash(git push *) and, on Windows, the PowerShell(git push *) twin, placed in managed settings so no session configuration can drop it. bypassPermissions skips prompts except those forced by explicit ask rules, so the push halts every time.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A PreToolUse hook returning permissionDecision "ask". It also forces the prompt, but it introduces a script whose crash is a non-blocking error indistinguishable from a clean pass, which is a worse posture for a gate that must never be missed.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. Permission rules are enforced by Claude Code rather than the model, and the precedence is one directional: a hook returning allow cannot suppress a matching ask rule.
sheets.context_boundary: The rule is evaluated in the harness on each Bash call. The model sees only that the call is awaiting approval; the human decision is taken in the CLI, never in the context window.
sheets.lifecycle: Evaluated on every Bash tool call for the whole session, in deny then ask then allow order, with the first match deciding. It stops applying only when the rule is removed from the settings file that carries it.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed on a match, but matching is textual, so a push spelled around the pattern (git -C repo push, a push inside a shell script or a make target, or gh) never matches and sails through the auto approving config. In dontAsk mode the call is denied outright rather than prompted, which is safe but not the requested behaviour.
sheets.version_caveat: No version gate on ask rules themselves. If the same gate is built as a hook instead, auto mode only honours a hook's ask reliably from v2.1.211; before that the classifier could approve an unsandboxed Bash command without showing the prompt the hook requested.

sheets.primary: An explicit ask rule in settings: "ask": ["Bash(git push *)"], placed in managed settings (or at minimum the committed project settings) so it cannot be edited away, plus PowerShell(git push *) on Windows fleets. Content-scoped ask rules are the documented exception that still forces a prompt under bypassPermissions and auto mode, and they survive a sandbox's autoAllowBashIfSandboxed substitution.
sheets.rejected_alternative: A PreToolUse hook returning permissionDecision "ask". It does fire in every permission mode and would work, but it is one more script that disableAllHooks or a hook-loading policy can suppress, whereas the ask rule's precedence is guaranteed by the permission engine.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness. Permission rules are evaluated by Claude Code before the tool runs; the model cannot approve its own push, and no permission mode the session was launched with removes an explicit ask rule.
sheets.context_boundary: Evaluated in the CLI process before execution. The confirmation happens in the terminal UI, entirely outside the context window; the model sees only the approved-or-denied outcome as its tool result.
sheets.lifecycle: Checked on every matching Bash call for the whole session. An ask rule never persists an approval, so it prompts each time rather than once per repository. It stops applying only if the rule is removed from the settings source that supplies it.
sheets.failure_mode: Fails closed for the literal pattern but is fragile at the edges, because Bash argument matching is string matching: git -C dir push, an aliased or wrapper-invoked push, devbox run git push, or a push buried inside a shell script the model executes will not match Bash(git push *). Two mode caveats also change the outcome rather than the safety: dontAsk mode denies instead of prompting, and a headless -p run has no human to answer so the call is refused.
sheets.version_caveat: No version gate on ask rules. Note the interaction documented for sandboxing: when the sandbox is enabled with autoAllowBashIfSandboxed left at true, a bare Bash ask rule is substituted away by the sandbox boundary, but a content-scoped rule like Bash(git push *) still forces the prompt, which is why the rule must be written with the specifier rather than as a whole-tool ask.

sheets.primary: A PreToolUse hook matched on Bash that parses the command, and when it resolves to a git push returns a structured decision asking for explicit confirmation (or denying with a reason that says to ask the human), since hooks are evaluated on the tool call itself rather than through the normal permission-prompt path.
sheets.rejected_alternative: An ask-style permission rule in settings.json for Bash(git push:*), which is the natural fit but is precisely what an auto-approving / bypass session skips.
sheets.enforcement_owner: The harness runs the hook and enforces its decision; the human owns the confirmation itself.
sheets.context_boundary: The hook process sees only the proposed command string and session metadata; the decision plus its reason cross back into the model's context, and the push never executes unless confirmed.
sheets.lifecycle: Evaluated before every Bash tool call for the whole session, no matter which approval mode the session was launched in; it stops applying only if the hook config is removed or hooks are disabled.
sheets.failure_mode: String matching on a shell command is the weak point and it fails open on anything unusual: git -C other/repo push, an alias, a push buried in a && chain or a heredoc, a Makefile target, a script that pushes, or a library call from Python. Match loosely and deny on ambiguity so the failure direction is closed, and accept the false positives.
sheets.version_caveat: Whether a PreToolUse hook can return an ask decision (as opposed to only allow or deny) and whether an ask decision still surfaces a prompt when the session was started with permission prompting bypassed are both version-dependent behaviours I cannot confirm from memory. If ask is not honoured under bypass, deny with an instructive reason is the reliable form.
